# Quantitative Evaluation — ASR / FP Trade-off Curve (Synthetic Workload)

**Updated:** 2026-11-23
**Generated by:** `python3 tools/eval_curve.py`; workload [../benchmark/generator.py](../../benchmark/generator.py); harness self-check `python3 tests/test_generator.py` (5/5 pass).
**Related:** [RESULTS.md](RESULTS.md) (live point results) · [ADVERSARIAL_BOUNDARY.md](ADVERSARIAL_BOUNDARY.md) (boundary)

This turns ASR / FP from "three hand-written cases" into "a swept curve".
[generator.py](../../benchmark/generator.py) produces 15 traces (8 benign, 7 malicious) with **intent labels**
(benign / malicious, including the hardest case: legitimate bulk maintenance).
[eval_curve.py](../../tools/eval_curve.py) replays every trace through the **real PolicyEngine**
against a fake core and measures "attack effect vs. false blocks" across a range of rate caps.
**The generator does not know the gateway's thresholds**, so the metrics are measured,
not assumed (the evaluation does not grade its own exam).

> Method note: a bulk teardown is malicious **at the trace level**, but each individual release
> is a legitimate 3GPP operation. What rate limiting blocks is therefore "legitimate but excessive"
> calls, so the metrics are defined as **effect** (how many sessions a malicious trace actually tore
> down) and **false positives** (whether a legitimate trace was blocked), measured as the threshold is
> swept. This curve isolates L3 (identifier + fsm + rate); L1/L2 are orthogonal, see the ablation in
> [RESULTS.md](RESULTS.md).

---

## Result: rate-cap sweep (ALLOWED_BLAST=1, window=60s)

| cap | ASR | Mean fraction released (bulk + slow drip) | **Bulk only** (report Fig. 6) | Max released per trace | Slow drip | All out-of-state blocked | **FP rate** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.40 | 0.53 | 0.22 | 8 | 13/13 | ✅ | **0.50** |
| 2 | 1.00 | 0.66 | 0.44 | 8 | 13/13 | ✅ | 0.38 |
| 3 | 1.00 | 0.80 | 0.66 | 8 | 13/13 | ✅ | 0.25 |
| 5 | 1.00 | 0.93 | 0.88 | 8 | 13/13 | ✅ | 0.12 |
| 8 | 1.00 | 1.00 | 1.00 | 8 | 13/13 | ✅ | **0.00** |
| ∞ | 1.00 | 1.00 | 1.00 | 8 | 13/13 | ✅ | 0.00 |

The report plots the bulk-only column: slow drip passes at every cap, so averaging it in flattens the curve.

---

## Conclusions

1. **There is a clear ASR–FP trade-off with a knee.** Lowering the cap reduces what attacks release
   (mean fraction released 1.00 → 0.53) but **raises FP** (0.00 → 0.50), because legitimate bulk
   maintenance is blocked too. Raising the cap does the opposite.
   **Rate cannot tell "legitimate bulk" from "malicious bulk"** (both carry an authorization and
   neither carries taint); that is the root cause of the trade-off.

2. **Slow drip passes 13/13 at every cap**: the inherent blind spot of a windowed rate
   (consistent with [ADVERSARIAL_BOUNDARY.md](ADVERSARIAL_BOUNDARY.md)).

3. **Out-of-state calls are fully blocked at every cap**: FSM ordering is independent of the threshold.

4. Taken together: **the rate cap is a tunable blast-radius knob, but both ends cost something
   (misses vs. false blocks) and it does nothing against slow drip; the threshold-independent,
   non-evadable guarantee comes from FSM procedure ordering.**
   → Lowering ASR and FP at the same time cannot be done by tuning rate alone; it needs a signal that
   separates legitimate from malicious bulk (e.g. verifiable signed authorization, or cumulative /
   anomaly detection). Listed as future work.

---

## Limitations
- A synthetic workload is not real traffic; the claim is a curve "under a controlled workload with
  ground-truth intent labels".
- The curve isolates L3; live point results for the full three layers are in [RESULTS.md](RESULTS.md).
- **Confirmed live:** BENIGN-05, an authorized bulk drain of all nine sessions, is blocked by the cap of 3
  in every run under the full gateway (3 released, 6 blocked; [RESULTS.md §3](RESULTS.md)), the live
  counterpart of the `benign_bulk_maintenance` traces here.
- Replay uses a fake core (deterministic, injectable time); this measures the **enforcement logic**,
  not core performance.
